original_question: For which Banach spaces X are the spaces ℓ_∞(X) and L_∞([0, 1], X) isomorphic?
target_in_paper: Section 5.2 (Structural properties), Problem 5.7 (Cembranos-Mendoza): "When are ℓ∞(X) and L∞([0,1],X) isomorphic?"
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper’s exact target problem almost verbatim: it identifies the correct pair of spaces, asks for a characterization of those Banach spaces X for which they are isomorphic, and does not drift to the neighboring but different Problems 5.5 and 5.6 about ℓ2(X), L2([0,1],X), and copies of ℓ2(X).
missing_details: The paper works throughout with real Banach spaces, so X should be understood as a real Banach space.
[0,1] is equipped with the Lebesgue measure λ.
L∞([0,1],X) means L∞(λ,X): the Banach space of λ-a.e. equivalence classes of essentially bounded, strongly measurable X-valued functions.
ℓ∞(X) should be understood as the Banach space of bounded X-valued sequences with the supremum norm.
"Isomorphic" should be made explicit as isomorphic as Banach spaces, i.e. via a bounded linear bijection with bounded inverse.
No separability assumption should be added: unlike Problems 5.5 and 5.6, Problem 5.7 is stated for arbitrary Banach spaces X.
refined_question: Characterize the real Banach spaces X for which the Banach spaces ℓ∞(X) and L∞([0,1],X)=L∞(λ,X) are isomorphic, where ℓ∞(X) is the space of bounded X-valued sequences with the supremum norm, [0,1] carries Lebesgue measure λ, and L∞(λ,X) consists of λ-a.e. equivalence classes of essentially bounded strongly measurable X-valued functions.
justification: The draft is targeting Problem 5.7 exactly. The nearby context in Section 5.2 introduces the vector-valued L∞ space and states the official problem in essentially the same words. To make it fully stand-alone and faithful to the paper, one must import the paper-wide convention that all Banach spaces are real, the global convention that [0,1] carries Lebesgue measure λ, and the local definition that L∞(μ,X) consists of equivalence classes of essentially bounded strongly measurable functions. It is also important not to add a separability restriction: the adjacent Problems 5.5 and 5.6 explicitly say "separable Banach spaces X," while Problem 5.7 does not.
